text: The initial supported platform is x86-64 desktop and laptop hardware only; no other architecture is a 1.0 requirement.
Decide the kernel strategy as a radical fork of the Linux kernel (ADR: fork vs new microkernel vs Linux-as-hypervisor), recording the rationale of hardware maturity vs native model.
The native model must be capability-based, component-oriented, asynchronous and object-based; every native ABI surface is checked against these four properties.
Provide a Linux/POSIX compatibility personality that runs existing Linux software.
Provide a Windows/Win32 compatibility personality that runs existing Windows software.
Decide the language policy: Rust for all new kernel and platform code, C retained only where inherited Linux code remains appropriate (ADR with criteria for when a C subsystem may be rewritten).
Establish Rust-in-kernel build support (toolchain, bindings, Kbuild integration) so native kernel subsystems can be written in Rust from V0.
Do not build another Linux distribution; the project identity and gating must reject distribution-style deliverables.
Do not build another desktop environment on top of an existing Linux userspace.
Do not build a Linux userspace with prettier APIs; native APIs must not be thin wrappers over Linux syscalls.
Do not make the native OS POSIX-compatible; POSIX exists only inside the Linux personality.
Do not build a Windows clone; Win32 exists only inside the Windows personality.
Do not pursue a traditional microkernel for academic purity; kernel residency of subsystems is decided by measured cost, not ideology.
Do not rewrite the kernel for the sake of rewriting it; every rewrite task must cite a semantic or measured benefit.
The OS must inherit Linux's mature hardware foundation while not inheriting Linux as the native programming model.
Retain Linux PCIe support in the forked kernel.
Retain Linux USB support in the forked kernel.
Retain Linux NVMe support in the forked kernel.
Retain Linux SATA support in the forked kernel.
Retain Linux ACPI support in the forked kernel.
Retain Linux power management in the forked kernel.
Retain Linux AMD, Intel and NVIDIA graphics driver support (DRM) in the forked kernel.
Retain Linux Wi-Fi driver support in the forked kernel.
Retain Linux Ethernet driver support in the forked kernel.
Retain Linux Bluetooth support in the forked kernel.
Retain Linux audio driver support (ALSA) in the forked kernel.
Retain Linux input device support in the forked kernel.
Retain Linux mature filesystem implementations in the forked kernel.
Retain Linux virtualization support (KVM) in the forked kernel.
Retain Linux x86-64 architecture support in the forked kernel.
Do not remove or break Linux ARM64 architecture support in the fork even though ARM64 is not an initial platform; keep a future port possible.
Do not remove or break Linux RISC-V architecture support in the fork; keep a future port possible.
Retain the thousands of inherited Linux hardware drivers; no fork change may regress a driver without an explicit decision.
POSIX is not the native API; no native SDK or ABI surface may be POSIX-shaped without independent justification.
Processes are not the fundamental native abstraction; Component replaces process as the unit of isolation.
File descriptors are not the universal object abstraction; typed Capability<T> handles replace them natively.
Paths are not the security model; no native authority check may be based on a filesystem path.
Threads are not the primary native concurrency abstraction; Task and TaskGroup are.
Signals are not the primary native notification mechanism; Operation completion and typed channels are.
Containers are not required for native isolation; Component and ResourceDomain provide isolation without a container runtime.
Native installation must not mutate a shared filesystem.
Native applications must not receive ambient access to the user's machine.
System state must not be an accumulation of mutable files; it is versioned generations plus explicit history.
AI must not operate by pretending to be a human moving a mouse; AI integration uses semantic interfaces and capabilities (see §42, §44).
The native platform must not assume hardware topology remains CPU + RAM + GPU forever (see §37, §38).
Define and implement Component as a fundamental native abstraction.
Define and implement Task as a fundamental native abstraction.
Define and implement TaskGroup as a fundamental native abstraction.
Define and implement Object<T> as the fundamental typed kernel object abstraction.
Define and implement Capability<T> as the fundamental userspace reference to kernel objects.
Define and implement Channel<T> as the fundamental typed IPC abstraction.
Define and implement MemoryObject as the fundamental large-data abstraction.
Define and implement ResourceDomain as the fundamental resource accounting and policy abstraction.
Define and implement Operation as the fundamental unit of asynchronous outstanding work.
Define and implement Package as the fundamental immutable software distribution abstraction.
Define and implement SystemGeneration as the fundamental versioned-OS-state abstraction.
Define and implement ComputeDevice as the fundamental heterogeneous execution resource abstraction.
Define and implement Interface<T> as the fundamental typed service contract abstraction.
Publish a vision document stating what the project is and is not building, as the top-level entry point of the repository.
Preserve mature Linux mechanisms and replace only inherited semantics; every subsystem task must classify its target as mechanism (keep) or semantics (replace).
Do not replace a mature subsystem merely because it is old.
Do not frame the project as 'rewrite Linux faster'; performance claims must come from semantic change, not reimplementation.
Preserve Linux page-table management as a mechanism the native memory model builds upon.
Preserve Linux memory allocators (page allocator, slab) as native mechanisms.
Preserve the Linux TCP/IP implementation as the network mechanism underneath native network objects.
Preserve Linux NVMe support as the storage mechanism underneath native storage objects.
Preserve Linux GPU drivers as the graphics mechanism underneath native Surface/Buffer objects.
Preserve Linux interrupt handling infrastructure unchanged in the fork.
Preserve Linux hardware discovery (bus enumeration, device model) unchanged in the fork.
ADR: replace the process model with Component; specify what native replaces PID, parent/child, exit status and process groups.
ADR: replace the thread model with Task/TaskGroup; specify how tasks map onto kernel execution contexts.
ADR: replace file descriptors with typed capability handles; specify the handle table design.
ADR: replace the global filesystem namespace with per-component capability-scoped storage objects.
ADR: fork() has no native equivalent; specify the native component-spawn primitive that replaces it.
ADR: signals have no native equivalent; specify how termination, cancellation and asynchronous notification are expressed natively.
ADR: ambient permissions are replaced by explicit capability grants; specify the grant sources (launcher, user choice, manifest).
ADR: package mutation is replaced by immutable packages and generations.
ADR: global dependency installation is replaced by immutable per-package dependency objects.
ADR: container-based isolation is replaced by Component + ResourceDomain; OCI containers become Linux-personality compatibility.
Compatibility personalities inherit history; native software does not. This firewall must be documented and enforced in ABI review.
Establish an ABI review gate that rejects any native interface justified only by a POSIX, Linux or Windows equivalent.
Linux personality must expose processes to Linux applications.
Linux personality must expose PIDs to Linux applications.
Linux personality must expose file descriptors to Linux applications.
Linux personality must expose POSIX signals to Linux applications.
Linux personality must expose /proc to Linux applications.
Linux personality must expose /sys to Linux applications.
Linux personality must expose BSD sockets to Linux applications.
Linux personality must support fork() for Linux applications.
Linux personality must support exec() for Linux applications.
Linux personality must support epoll for Linux applications.
Linux personality must expose POSIX paths to Linux applications.
Linux personality must expose the Linux syscall ABI to Linux applications.
Windows personality must expose Win32 APIs to Windows applications.
Windows personality must expose NT object semantics to Windows applications.
Windows personality must expose Windows process semantics to Windows applications.
Windows personality must expose Windows handles to Windows applications.
Windows personality must expose DirectX to Windows applications.
Windows personality must expose Windows filesystem semantics to Windows applications.
Windows personality must expose registry semantics to Windows applications.
Native applications must see none of the Linux or Windows constructs unless explicitly using a compatibility environment.
Resolve how a native application explicitly opts into a compatibility environment (capability to a personality, embedded Linux component, or SDK shim) and what authority that grants.
Native kernel interfaces must never exist merely because POSIX, Linux or Windows has an equivalent concept.
Native applications execute against the Native Platform layer (SDK + platform services) rather than the kernel directly.
Linux applications execute through a Linux ABI Personality layer.
Windows applications execute through a Win32/NT Personality layer.
All three application paths (native, Linux personality, Windows personality) terminate in Native Kernel Objects; personalities ultimately sit above native primitives.
UI is a user-space service above native kernel objects (compositor, UI protocol).
Storage is a user-space service above native kernel objects.
Network is a user-space service above native kernel objects (network capability broker), while the TCP stack stays in the kernel.
Kernel Core owns memory management as a native kernel responsibility.
Kernel Core owns IPC (channel transport) as a native kernel responsibility.
Kernel Core owns capability enforcement as a native kernel responsibility.
Kernel Core owns scheduling as a native kernel responsibility.
A Linux-derived hardware layer (drivers, buses) sits beneath the kernel core and is retained from upstream.
Publish the high-level architecture diagram and layer definitions as a maintained document with each layer's owning workstream.
ADR: which services are user-space (UI, Storage, Network) vs kernel core (Memory, IPC, Capabilities, Scheduler), with criteria for moving a service across the boundary.
ADR: select the contemporary Linux kernel version and tree (mainline vs LTS) to fork, with rebase cadence.
Create the kernel fork repository with upstream remote, patch tracking and a documented rebase workflow.
Preserve Linux boot (early init, initramfs handoff) in the fork initially.
Preserve Linux architecture support code in the fork initially.
Preserve Linux interrupt subsystem in the fork initially.
Preserve Linux memory-management internals in the fork initially.
Preserve the Linux scheduler in the fork initially; native scheduling intent layers on top.
Preserve Linux PCI subsystem in the fork initially.
Preserve Linux USB subsystem in the fork initially.
Preserve Linux ACPI subsystem in the fork initially.
Preserve Linux DRM/KMS in the fork initially.
Preserve Linux networking drivers in the fork initially.
Preserve Linux storage drivers in the fork initially.
Preserve Linux input subsystem in the fork initially.
Preserve Linux Bluetooth subsystem in the fork initially.
Preserve KVM in the fork initially.
Preserve Linux hardware discovery in the fork initially.
Preserve Linux firmware loading in the fork initially.
Preserve Linux power management in the fork initially.
Preserve mature Linux filesystems (ext4, btrfs, xfs, vfat) in the fork initially.
Do not attempt a heroic kernel rewrite; the V0 objective is adding the native model alongside retained Linux facilities.
Boot the forked kernel unmodified in behaviour on QEMU and on the reference x86-64 hardware as the first kernel task.
Phase A: keep the fork reasonably close to upstream while adding the native platform alongside Linux facilities.
Phase A: Linux applications must continue functioning normally on the fork; add a regression suite of Linux binaries that must pass on every kernel build.
Phase B: establish two execution worlds, Native ABI and Linux ABI, selectable per component/process.
Phase B: native applications must not depend on Linux syscall semantics; verify with a syscall-filter that native components cannot invoke Linux syscalls.
Phase B: Linux becomes a compatibility personality with its own entry path rather than the default execution model.
Phase C (initial): implement native Component as a wrapper around task_struct, mm_struct, namespaces and cgroups.
Phase C (later): replace the wrapper implementation of Component with a native kernel implementation while keeping the ABI unchanged.
The native abstraction must stay ABI-stable while its kernel implementation evolves from Linux wrappers to native code; ABI conformance tests must pass across both implementations.
ADR: Phase D entry criteria—when full upstream merges stop being mandatory and controlled divergence begins.
Phase D: process for adapting upstream driver improvements into the diverged kernel.
Phase D: process for adapting upstream security fixes (CVE backport pipeline) into the diverged kernel.
Phase D: process for adapting upstream architecture improvements into the diverged kernel.
Phase D: process for adopting upstream algorithms, scheduler ideas and memory-management improvements selectively.
Phase D: process for adapting upstream subsystem patches rather than blind merging.
Phase E: reach a kernel no longer reasonably described as Linux, with independent native ABI, execution model, security model, IPC architecture and system semantics.
Resolve which kernel evolution phase (C, D or E) is a hard requirement for the 1.0 release gate.
Write and maintain the kernel divergence policy document defining phases A–E, their gates and what upstream tracking each phase requires.
Build upstream-tracking tooling that reports patch delta, conflict hot-spots and unmerged upstream security fixes.
The native kernel must expose typed objects Object<T> with a type identifier checked on every operation.
Define Object<File>.
Define Object<Directory>.
Define Object<Channel<Message>>.
Define Object<Surface>.
Define Object<Memory> (MemoryObject).
Define Object<ComputeQueue>.
Define Object<NetworkConnection>.
Define Object<AudioStream>.
Define Object<Camera>.
Define Object<Component>.
Define Object<TaskGroup>.
Define Object<Device>.
Define Object<Package>.
ADR: which Object<T> types are implemented in the kernel and which are user-service objects reached through channels, with the criteria for kernel residency.
Userspace receives Capability<T> handles rather than object pointers; implement the per-component capability table.
A capability must identify what object is referenced.
A capability must encode which operations the holder may perform (rights).
A capability must encode how the object may be transferred or delegated (transfer rights).
Capabilities must be unforgeable; userspace cannot mint a valid capability without the kernel.
Capabilities must be typed; using a Capability<File> where Capability<Channel> is expected must fail at the kernel boundary.
Capabilities must be transferable where permitted (send over channel, pass at component creation).
Capabilities must be revocable where appropriate; implement revocation that invalidates all derived capabilities.
Capabilities must be attenuable; implement derivation that only removes rights.
Capabilities must be inspectable; a holder can query type, rights and object identity of its own capabilities.
Capabilities must be auditable; every grant, derivation, transfer and revocation emits a trace event.
Capability<File, ReadWrite> may derive Capability<File, Read> but never Capability<File, Admin>; add a regression test for rights monotonicity.
ADR: rights representation (generic bitmask vs per-object-type typed rights vs rights as separate objects) including how Admin authority is expressed.
ADR: capability handle representation in userspace (dense index, sparse id, sealed value) and its implications for hardware-assisted enforcement.
Resolve revocation semantics: eager vs lazy invalidation, revocation of in-flight operations, and cost bounds on revocation trees.
The capability design must not assume software-only enforcement; the ABI specification must reserve room for hardware-enforced capabilities.
Study CHERI-like capability pointers and document how Capability<T> would map onto them.
Study tagged memory architectures and their implications for MemoryObject and capability storage.
Study bounds-enforced pointers and whether the ABI can express bounded views of MemoryObjects.
Study hardware provenance tracking and its fit with capability audit.
Study hardware memory capabilities as an enforcement backend for MemoryObject mappings.
Study secure enclaves (SGX/SEV-style) as a possible home for components requiring hardware confidentiality.
Study future memory-safe CPU architectures and record ABI assumptions that would break on them.
Application-visible capabilities must remain conceptually stable whether enforced by kernel metadata, page tables, CPU tags, hardware capabilities or combinations.
Define an enforcement-backend abstraction inside the kernel so capability checks can be implemented by kernel metadata today and hardware later.
Do not freeze the OS around the security limitations of current x86-64 hardware; ABI review must flag any x86-64-specific assumption.
Write a hardware-assisted capability readiness ADR listing the ABI invariants that must hold for future hardware enforcement.
No ambient authority: a native component starts with exactly the capabilities it was handed and nothing else.
A native application must not automatically receive filesystem access; add a conformance test.
A native application must not automatically receive home directory access.
A native application must not automatically receive network access.
A native application must not automatically receive camera access.
A native application must not automatically receive microphone access.
A native application must not automatically be able to enumerate other processes or components.
A native application must not automatically receive device access.
A native application must not automatically receive clipboard access.
A native application must not automatically receive location access.
A native application must not automatically receive screen contents.
A native application must not automatically receive other applications' data.
Packages declare a small initial capability set (RequestedCapabilities) that the launcher grants at start.
Define the UI capability that a launched application receives (window creation without screen contents).
Define the GPU capability that a launched application receives (render/compute queues without other surfaces).
Define the temporary-storage capability that a launched application receives (scratch storage scoped to the component).
The OS-owned chooser returns a Capability<Image, ReadWrite> for the object the user selected.
Selecting one file must never require granting access to the containing directory (e.g. ~/Pictures).
ADR: which authority sources exist (manifest request, launcher policy, user chooser, permissions UI, delegation from another component) and their precedence.
Worked PhotoEditor capability example must ship as an SDK sample and as an integration test proving the denied capabilities are absent.
Component is the primary isolation primitive of the native model.
A Component contains Code (mapped immutable executable objects).
A Component contains an AddressSpace.
A Component contains a Capabilities table.
A Component declares typed Inputs<T> (receiving channel endpoints).
A Component declares typed Outputs<T> (sending channel endpoints).
A Component owns a TaskGroup.
A Component belongs to a ResourceDomain.
Component creation must be extremely cheap: target tens to hundreds of microseconds, measured and tracked per build.
Isolation must be cheap enough that 'isolate it' is the default; SDK defaults create separate components without asking.
Prototype and measure the dominant costs of component creation (address-space setup, page-table population, capability table, scheduler registration) on the Linux wrapper implementation.
ADR: whether every Component gets its own address space or lightweight in-address-space components exist (relation to Wasm components).
Benchmark: component creation latency and memory overhead with comparison against Linux fork/exec, clone and container start.
Native applications are component graphs; the package format must describe multiple components and their connections.
Support a browser-shaped graph: a UI component, a Network component, per-Tab Renderer and JavaScript Runtime components, and a Download Manager component.
Each component in a graph receives only the authority it requires; the graph description must be capability-explicit per component.
ImageDecoder reference component: Input<ImageBytes>, Output<Bitmap>, memory budget 256 MB, CPU budget 25%.
Per-component memory budget enforcement via ResourceDomain.
Per-component CPU share enforcement via ResourceDomain.
ImageDecoder must have no network access; verify with an integration test.
ImageDecoder must have no arbitrary filesystem access; verify with an integration test.
ImageDecoder must have no microphone access.
ImageDecoder must have no process enumeration.
ImageDecoder must have no package installation authority.
An exploit must compromise only the smallest useful unit of software; the threat model must evaluate blast radius per component.
ADR: component graphs declared statically in the manifest vs instantiated dynamically at runtime by a parent component, and how dynamic children are constrained.
Inspect an application's live component graph (components, channels, capabilities) via os inspect.
The component ABI must be designed for long-term evolution; every interface definition carries an explicit evolution strategy.
Component ABI supports typed interfaces.
Component ABI supports interface versioning.
Component ABI supports optional methods.
Component ABI supports backwards-compatible schema evolution (adding fields without breaking old receivers).
Component ABI supports forwards-compatible extension (old senders understood by new receivers, unknown fields preserved).
Component ABI supports feature negotiation between endpoints.
Component ABI supports asynchronous methods.
Component ABI supports streams (multi-value results).
Component ABI supports futures (single deferred results).
Component ABI supports ownership transfer of capabilities and MemoryObjects in messages.
Component ABI supports cancellation of in-flight calls.
Component ABI defines failure semantics (error types, peer death, timeout).
Do not ship a typed IPC system without a simultaneously designed interface-evolution story; the IDL ADR must include evolution rules.
ADR: choose or design the IDL (new IDL vs WIT vs FIDL-derived) covering versioning, optional methods and extension.
Publish interface evolution guidelines for SDK authors, including compatibility test tooling that diffs two interface versions.
Study the WebAssembly Component Model and WASI as architectural inputs to the native component and interface model; document adopted and rejected ideas.
Do not duplicate concepts that already have strong ecosystem momentum (e.g. WIT, WASI interfaces) without justification.
Support both native machine-code components and portable WebAssembly components as component kinds.
Wasm is a first-class format for plugins.
Wasm is a first-class format for sandboxed extensions.
Wasm is a first-class format for portable services.
Wasm is a first-class format for automation modules (see §45).
Wasm is a first-class format for downloaded components.
Wasm is a first-class format for cross-architecture workloads.
Do not make Wasm the native machine ABI.
Maximum-performance native software must remain free to compile directly to machine code.
The native component model must map cleanly enough that Wasm components participate in the same object/capability/interface ecosystem (capabilities as WASI resources, channels as WIT interfaces).
ADR: choose the Wasm runtime (wasmtime, wasmer, custom) and whether it runs in-component or as a shared service.
ADR: relationship between the native IDL and WIT (same language, bidirectional mapping, or independent).
IPC is one of the highest-priority performance subsystems; IPC benchmarks gate every milestone.
Implement Channel<T> as the primary IPC abstraction with typed message payloads (e.g. Channel<ImageDecodeRequest>).
Services expose typed interfaces declared in the IDL (e.g. interface ImageDecoder { async decode(Image) -> Bitmap; }).
Ship the ImageDecoder interface and service as the reference typed service used by the V0 demo.
Native IPC is not sockets.
Native IPC is not untyped byte[] payloads.
Native IPC does not use arbitrary per-service serialization formats.
Native IPC does not use hand-written protocols.
Native IPC does not duplicate schemas on both sides; the IDL is the single source.
IDL tooling generates the wire representation.
IDL tooling generates client and server stubs.
IDL tooling generates ownership semantics (which parameters move, borrow or share).
IDL tooling generates version negotiation code.
IDL tooling generates tracing metadata so every call is observable by name and type.
ADR: wire format for typed messages (fixed layout, self-describing, schema-indexed) and its zero-copy properties.
Implement the IDL compiler with Rust as the first target language.
Implement a minimal-copy fast path for small messages between sender and receiver.
Prototype shared ring buffers as a small-message transport and measure round-trip latency.
Prototype register transfer of small messages during a scheduler handoff and measure latency.
Prototype scheduler-aware handoff (direct switch to receiver) and measure latency and fairness effects.
Prototype batched submission of messages and measure throughput gains.
Prototype lock-free queues for cross-core channel delivery and measure cross-core latency.
ADR: select the small-message fast path technique(s) from the prototyped options based on measurements.
Large payloads transfer by passing a MemoryObject capability from Component A to Component B rather than copying bytes.
Payload bytes must not move when avoidable; the IDL must make MemoryObject transfer the natural encoding for large data.
Resolve the size threshold and heuristics for inline small message vs MemoryObject transfer.
Benchmark small-message IPC round-trip latency (same core and cross core) against Linux pipes, Unix sockets, io_uring and Fuchsia/seL4 published numbers.
Benchmark large-payload MemoryObject transfer cost versus memcpy and versus Linux shared memory + fd passing.
Implement MemoryObject as the representation of large data with kernel-tracked properties and mappings.
MemoryObject supports the writable property.
MemoryObject supports the immutable property (sealing).
MemoryObject supports the shared property (multiple concurrent mappers).
MemoryObject supports copy-on-write.
MemoryObject supports the DMA-compatible property (physically contiguous or IOMMU-mappable).
MemoryObject supports the GPU-compatible property (importable by the GPU driver).
MemoryObject supports the executable property with W^X enforcement.
MemoryObject supports the persistent property (backed by durable storage).
MemoryObject supports the pinned property (never swapped or migrated).
MemoryObject supports the encrypted property.
Memory movement must prefer capability/ownership transfer over copying; SDK APIs default to move semantics for MemoryObjects.
ADR: MemoryObject kernel implementation basis (shmem/memfd, dma-buf, new object) and how it interoperates with Linux dma-buf for GPU/DMA.
Resolve semantics of persistent MemoryObjects: relation to the storage model, crash consistency, and content addressing.
Resolve semantics of encrypted MemoryObjects: key ownership, who can map plaintext, and interaction with hardware memory encryption.
MemoryObject properties must be inspectable and traced (creation, mapping, transfer, property changes).
Avoid the traditional copy pipeline (kernel buffer → application → decoder → graphics → GPU); each avoidable copy in a native data path is a defect to be measured and removed.
NIC DMA delivers directly into a MemoryObject.
A MemoryObject received from the network is transferred by ownership to a Decoder component without copying.
A Decoder output MemoryObject is transferred by ownership to a Renderer component without copying.
A Renderer hands a MemoryObject to the GPU without copying (GPU import of the same physical pages).
Demonstrate the same underlying physical memory used from NIC to GPU where hardware permits, and measure copies per stage.
The system understands MemoryObject ownership (single owner at a time).
The system understands borrowing (temporary access that returns to the owner).
The system understands sharing (multiple readers with defined coherence).
The system understands immutable mappings.
The system understands copy-on-write mappings.
The system understands DMA suitability of a MemoryObject.
The system understands device locality of a MemoryObject (which device's memory it lives in).
The system understands NUMA locality of a MemoryObject.
The system understands GPU accessibility of a MemoryObject.
Investigate NIC-to-MemoryObject DMA feasibility on retained Linux drivers (AF_XDP/zero-copy receive paths) and document constraints.
Investigate dma-buf interoperability between MemoryObject and the DRM drivers for zero-copy GPU import.
Resolve how borrowing lifetimes are enforced across component boundaries (revocation on return, timeouts, or trust in the borrower).
Benchmark the V0 demo pipeline (Component A → Channel<Request> → Component B → MemoryObject transfer → result) for copies, latency and memory overhead.
All native kernel APIs must be asynchronous by default; no native syscall may block the calling execution context as its primary mode.
Do not expose a blocking read()/write() thread-per-call model (block thread, wake thread) as the native I/O interface.
The kernel must expose a submit(operation) primitive that enqueues an Operation for asynchronous execution and returns without waiting for completion.
The kernel must expose a completion delivery mechanism through which finished Operations report results back to the submitting task.

Decide the submission/completion transport for Operations: shared submission and completion rings (io_uring-style), per-Component queues, syscall-per-operation, or a hybrid, and how batching of submissions is expressed.
Decide whether Operations that can complete synchronously (e.g. cached reads) are allowed to complete inline at submit time and how the ABI signals inline completion.
The kernel must support a Read Operation kind against readable objects (File, Channel, MemoryObject-backed sources).
The kernel must support a Write Operation kind against writable objects.
The kernel must support a Receive Operation kind for taking a typed message from a Channel<T>.
The kernel must support a Send Operation kind for placing a typed message on a Channel<T>.
The kernel must support a Connect Operation kind for establishing a connection to a service or NetworkConnection object.
The kernel must support an Accept Operation kind for receiving inbound connections on a listening object.
The kernel must support a Timer Operation kind that completes at or after an absolute or relative deadline.
The kernel must support a Wait Operation kind that completes when a referenced object or set of objects reaches a signalled state.
The kernel must support a GPUDispatch Operation kind that submits work to a ComputeQueue or RenderQueue and completes when the GPU signals completion.
The kernel must support a DeviceOperation Operation kind for asynchronous requests to Object<Device> instances (including user-space driver backed devices).
The kernel must support a StorageTransaction Operation kind that atomically applies a group of storage changes and completes on commit or abort.

Decide whether the Operation kind set (Read, Write, Receive, Send, Connect, Accept, Timer, Wait, GPUDispatch, DeviceOperation, StorageTransaction) is a closed kernel enum or an extensible registry that user-space services can add to, given ABI stability rules.
Operation completion must integrate directly with task scheduling so that the task awaiting an Operation is made runnable by the completion without a separate polling or wakeup syscall.
Measure submit-to-completion latency for a no-op Operation and for Timer/Wait Operations, and track it as a standing benchmark.
The tiny native runtime (cross-ref §59) must provide an async executor that drives futures from Operation completions without wrapping blocking Linux syscalls.
The kernel must expose Operation<Result> as a first-class typed object representing one unit of outstanding asynchronous work.
Every Operation must support cancellation by its owner, with a defined result (Cancelled) delivered through the normal completion path.
Every Operation must support completion notification carrying a typed Result or a typed failure.
Every Operation must support a deadline after which it is cancelled or fails with a deadline-exceeded result.
Every Operation must carry a priority that the kernel may use when ordering I/O, IPC, and scheduling work.
Every Operation must carry tracing metadata (identity, submitter, parent span) so its lifecycle is visible to the observability layer.
Every Operation must have an owner (a Task or TaskGroup) so that ownership can be transferred and cancelled structurally.
Every Operation must be attributed to a ResourceDomain for resource accounting of CPU, I/O, and memory it consumes.
The SDK must expose operation.cancel() as the cancellation entry point for an outstanding Operation.
The SDK must expose operation.deadline(...) to attach or modify a deadline on an outstanding Operation.
The SDK must expose operation.await so an Operation integrates with Rust async/await and suspends the owning Task until completion.
The kernel must maintain a uniform inspectable representation of all outstanding Operations so tooling can enumerate in-flight work per Task, Component, and ResourceDomain (cross-ref §64 os inspect).
Decide how an Operation is identified and referenced from user space: as a Capability<Operation>, as an index in the submission ring, or as an opaque handle with a separate cancellation token.

Define cancellation semantics for Operations already committed to hardware (in-flight DMA, GPU dispatch, network send): whether cancel waits, fails, or returns best-effort, and how partially completed results are reported.
Decide the failure encoding for Operation results (typed error enum per Operation kind vs uniform error object) so failure semantics are stable across the ABI.
Prototype deadline enforcement inside the kernel (timer wheel vs hrtimer per Operation) and measure overhead of per-Operation deadlines at high submission rates.
Native applications must be able to create enormous numbers of lightweight Tasks without corresponding kernel thread creation.
Demonstrate 500,000 concurrent Tasks in one Component without 500,000 kernel threads, and measure memory per Task and creation latency.
The kernel and native runtime must cooperate to multiplex Tasks across a bounded set of execution contexts (M:N scheduling).

Decide the kernel/runtime split for task multiplexing: which scheduling decisions live in the kernel (execution contexts, blocking notification) and which in the user-space runtime (task selection, work stealing).
Decide whether every Task has kernel-visible identity (Object<Task>) or only runtime identity with kernel visibility for observability and cancellation purposes.
The runtime must support an async fn programming model in which awaiting a database.get() or request.respond() style operation suspends only the Task, not the execution context.
The platform must record which specific Operation a suspended Task is waiting on, so the waiting relationship is inspectable (cross-ref §64 'Waiting: Channel<ImageDecodeRequest>').
Measure Task creation latency and Task switch latency and track them as standing benchmarks against Tokio tasks, Go goroutines, and Linux threads (cross-ref §54).
Study how execution-context blocking inside inherited Linux kernel paths (page faults, synchronous driver calls) is detected and compensated so a blocked context does not starve multiplexed Tasks.
Define how Linux personality threads and Windows personality threads map onto native Tasks and execution contexts (cross-ref LNX, WIN).
The kernel must model Task ownership as a hierarchy: Application owns TaskGroups, TaskGroups own Tasks, and Components own their own TaskGroup.
TaskGroup must be a kernel object (Object<TaskGroup>) that can be referenced by capability and can own Tasks and child TaskGroups.
Cancellation must propagate down the ownership hierarchy: cancelling a TaskGroup cancels all owned Tasks, child TaskGroups, and their outstanding Operations.
app.cancel() must deterministically cancel all work owned by the application and complete only after every owned Task has terminated.
Persistent background execution beyond the lifetime of the owning application must require an explicit capability (e.g. Capability<BackgroundExecution>).
No Task may outlive its owning TaskGroup without the background-execution capability; the system must make accidental orphan processes impossible.
Write a regression test that verifies no Task survives cancellation of its TaskGroup and that no orphan Task exists after application exit.
Define cleanup semantics for cancelled Tasks holding capabilities, MemoryObjects, or partially transferred ownership: whether resources are released immediately, on Task exit, or by the owner.
Define how cancellation interacts with a Task blocked in an inherited Linux kernel path that cannot be interrupted (uninterruptible sleep).
Decide whether cancellation is cooperative (Task observes a cancellation flag at await points) or forced (kernel tears down the Task), or a staged combination with a grace deadline.
The observability layer must expose the TaskGroup ownership tree (which TaskGroup owns which Tasks and Components).
The native scheduler interface must express scheduling intent rather than only a generic numeric priority.
Both ResourceDomain and individual Tasks must be able to declare a scheduling intent.
The scheduler must support an Interactive intent class for work that must respond promptly to user input.
The scheduler must support a Background intent class for deferrable work that yields to everything else.
The scheduler must support a Throughput intent class for batch work that maximises total progress.
The scheduler must support a LowLatency intent class for work that must be scheduled with minimal wakeup delay.
The scheduler must support a Realtime intent class with bounded scheduling latency guarantees.
The scheduler must support an EnergyEfficient intent class that trades latency for lower power consumption.
The scheduler must support a Deadline intent class in which work declares a completion deadline and period.
Audio rendering must be schedulable under strict low-latency intent; validate with an audio-callback jitter test (cross-ref AUD).
The compositor must run under interactive/deadline-sensitive intent aligned with display vblank (cross-ref GFX).
Game render threads (including Windows personality games) must be able to run under latency-sensitive intent (cross-ref WIN).
Compilers and build jobs must be schedulable under throughput intent without degrading interactive work; validate with a compile-while-typing test.
Indexing services must run under background intent and be preempted by any interactive work.
Battery-powered sync tasks must run under energy-efficient intent that prefers efficient cores and lower frequencies.
Scheduling intent must influence CPU scheduling class and placement decisions.
Scheduling intent must influence GPU scheduling priority for RenderQueue and ComputeQueue submissions (cross-ref GFX, HET).
Scheduling intent must influence CPU frequency scaling (cpufreq/EPP hints) so latency-sensitive work is not throttled and background work is.
Scheduling intent must influence core selection on heterogeneous CPUs (performance vs efficiency cores, SMT siblings).
Scheduling intent must influence memory placement (NUMA node, GPU-local vs host memory) for the domain's allocations (cross-ref MEM).
Scheduling intent must influence I/O scheduling priority for storage and network Operations submitted by the domain.

Decide how intents map onto inherited Linux scheduler mechanisms (EEVDF/CFS nice and latency-nice, SCHED_DEADLINE, SCHED_FIFO/RR, uclamp, cgroup cpu controllers) versus introducing a native scheduling class.
Evaluate whether Linux EEVDF plus uclamp and cgroup controllers can adequately express the seven intent classes before committing to scheduler modifications.
Define which intents (Realtime, LowLatency) require a capability to request and how the system prevents an unprivileged Component from starving others.
Define intent and priority inheritance across Channel handoff so a LowLatency client calling a shared service does not queue behind Background work in the service.
Measure wakeup-to-run scheduling latency per intent class under load and track it as a standing benchmark.
Resource accounting must be a native kernel concept applied to every Component and Task, not an optional add-on.
The kernel must expose ResourceDomain as a kernel object referenced by capability.

ResourceDomain must carry a memory budget with enforcement when exceeded.
ResourceDomain must carry a GPU budget (time share and memory) enforced through the graphics and compute queues.
ResourceDomain must carry an I/O budget (bandwidth and IOPS) for storage Operations.
ResourceDomain must carry a network policy (allowed connectivity, bandwidth) applied to network capabilities (cross-ref NET).
ResourceDomain must carry a storage quota applied to the domain's persistent objects (cross-ref STO).
ResourceDomain must carry an energy policy influencing frequency scaling and core selection for the domain.
ResourceDomain must carry a latency policy that sets default scheduling intent and deadlines for member Tasks.
Every Component and application must belong to exactly one ResourceDomain at creation, inherited from or assigned by its creator.
Decide whether ResourceDomains are hierarchical (nested budgets with parent enforcement) or flat, and how budgets are delegated and attenuated via capabilities.
Decide the initial implementation of ResourceDomain as a wrapper over cgroups v2 controllers (cpu, memory, io, pids) per §6 Phase C, and record the migration path to a native implementation.
ResourceDomain must subsume the isolation and accounting roles of cgroups so native software never configures cgroups directly.
ResourceDomain plus Component capability sets must subsume the roles of Linux namespaces for native software (mount, pid, net, user, ipc).
ResourceDomain plus Component creation must replace container runtimes as the native isolation mechanism (cross-ref §36).
ResourceDomain policy must replace per-application scheduler configuration (nice, chrt, cpuset tuning) for native software.
ResourceDomain GPU budget must replace vendor-specific GPU control interfaces for native software.
Define behaviour on budget exhaustion within a ResourceDomain: memory reclaim, throttling, Operation failure, or Component termination, and how it is reported to the owner.
Investigate whether GPU time and memory budgets can be enforced with current DRM scheduler and cgroup GPU controller support for AMD, Intel, and NVIDIA drivers.
Resource consumption per ResourceDomain must be readable through the observability layer and os inspect resource (cross-ref §64).
Measure ResourceDomain creation and teardown latency and track it as a standing benchmark (a component of isolation cost in §53).
Every major OS primitive must be observable as an architectural requirement, not as debugging glue added later.
Components must be observable: creation, state, owner, capabilities, resource use.
Tasks must be observable: creation, owner TaskGroup, state, waiting-on Operation.
TaskGroups must be observable: membership, hierarchy, cancellation state.
Channels must be observable: endpoints, message type, queue depth, throughput, blocked senders and receivers.
Capabilities must be observable: holder, target object, rights, derivation chain, revocation state.
Operations must be observable: kind, submitter, submission time, state, deadline, completion latency.
MemoryObjects must be observable: size, properties, current owner, mappings, transfer history.
ResourceDomains must be observable: budgets, current consumption, members, throttling events.
ComputeQueues must be observable: pending dispatches, device, queue latency, completions.
The observability layer must expose creation events for every primitive.
The observability layer must expose ownership of every primitive.
The observability layer must expose relationships between primitives (which Component holds which Channel, which Task owns which Operation).
The observability layer must expose resource use per primitive.
The observability layer must expose latency measurements for Operations, IPC, and scheduling.
The observability layer must expose queueing (Channel depth, run-queue wait, Operation backlog).
The observability layer must expose failures (Operation errors, Component crashes, revocations).
The observability layer must expose capability grants as auditable events (cross-ref CAP audit).
The observability layer must expose IPC flow between Components as a traceable graph.
The observability layer must expose scheduling delays (wakeup-to-run per Task and intent class).
Tracing must impose extremely low overhead; measure the cost of disabled tracepoints and of enabled tracing on IPC round-trip and Task switch, and set a budget.
Trace events must be structured (typed fields, not free-form strings).
Trace events must be semantic, named in terms of OS primitives (Channel send, Operation complete) rather than raw kernel internals.
Tracing must be dynamically enabled and disabled at runtime per primitive, per Component, or per ResourceDomain without restart.
Tracing must be security-aware: reading traces of another Component requires a capability, and trace payloads must not leak message contents without explicit authority.
Tooling must not need to reconstruct application semantics from raw kernel events when the OS already knows the semantic relationship; primitives must emit semantic events directly.
Decide the tracing infrastructure: extend inherited ftrace/tracepoints/eBPF, build a native structured trace ring per Component, or layer a native semantic schema over eBPF.
Decide the trace event schema and export format (binary ring format, Perfetto/CTF compatibility, OpenTelemetry mapping) so external tools can consume traces.
IDL code generation must emit tracing metadata for every typed interface method so IPC calls appear as semantic spans (cross-ref §14).
Provide a trace viewer or exporter usable from os trace (cross-ref §64) to inspect Component, Task, Channel, and Operation timelines.
Study eBPF, Fuchsia tracing, and Perfetto to determine which semantic tracing capabilities the native layer should provide natively versus via retained Linux tooling.
Humans must continue to see files and folders in the user-facing storage model.
Native applications must not receive a universal filesystem namespace by default.
The kernel or storage service must expose File as a typed object accessible only via Capability<File, Rights>.
The storage model must expose Directory as a typed object whose capability scopes access to its subtree.
The storage model must expose Collection as a typed object representing a user-meaningful group of items (e.g. a photo album) independent of directory layout.
The storage model must expose Blob as a typed immutable byte object, preferably content-addressed (cross-ref §27).
The storage model must expose PackageData as read-only access to a package's bundled resources.
The storage model must expose ApplicationData as per-application private persistent storage granted by default without user prompt.
The storage model must expose UserSelected<T> as the type of objects returned by an OS chooser, carrying the granted authority.
The SDK must expose files.choose<T>() returning a typed UserSelected<T> capability after the user selects an object.
Build the file chooser as an OS-owned privileged service that holds broad storage authority and hands out narrow capabilities to applications.
The object returned by the chooser must itself carry the authority (capability), so no path-based permission check follows selection.
Write a verification test that an application using files.choose<Image>() can read the chosen image while holding no capability to /home/<user>/Pictures or any directory.
Decide how the type parameter of choose<T> (Image, Document, Directory) maps to content types and how the chooser filters and validates selections.
Define persistent grants: how an application retains access to a user-selected object across restarts (durable capability, recent-files list) and how the user revokes it.
Define the save-as flow: how an application obtains authority to create a new file in a user-chosen location without directory access.
Define how the Linux and Windows personalities present native storage objects as POSIX paths and Windows drive letters while respecting capability scope (cross-ref LNX, WIN).
Native file browser application must operate as a privileged holder of user storage authority and be able to hand capabilities to other apps via drag/drop (cross-ref §60, UIP).
Storage must support copy-on-write semantics for files and objects.
Storage must support snapshots of subtrees and of the whole system volume.
Storage must support deduplication of identical content.
Storage must support checksums on data and metadata with detection of corruption on read.
Storage must support immutable versions of objects that cannot be modified once sealed.
Storage must support cheap clones (reflink) of files and trees.
Storage must support atomic replacement of a file or tree so readers never observe a partial update.
Storage must support transactions grouping multiple changes with all-or-nothing commit (backs StorageTransaction Operation in §18).
Storage must support integrity verification of stored objects against expected content hashes on demand and at boot for system generations.
Decide the initial underlying Linux filesystem for the native storage layer (btrfs, bcachefs, ZFS, XFS with reflink plus overlay) against the nine storage requirements.
Do not write a new filesystem merely because the OS is new; the initial implementation must sit over a mature Linux filesystem.
Define the criteria (semantic gaps, measured performance shortfalls) under which a native filesystem or object store would be justified, and re-evaluate at each milestone gate.
Benchmark candidate filesystems for snapshot creation time, clone time, checksum overhead, and dedup effectiveness on a representative system image.
Build the native storage service as a user-space component that mediates capability-scoped access to the underlying filesystem (cross-ref §4 User Services: Storage).
Immutable data must be identifiable by content hash using an identifier form such as sha256:<hex>.
Decide the content-hash algorithm and identifier format (SHA-256 vs BLAKE3, multihash prefix, chunking scheme for large objects) and its upgrade path.
Build a content-addressed object store service that stores, retrieves, and reference-counts immutable objects by hash.
The content-addressed store must deduplicate identical objects across packages, generations, and caches.
The content-addressed store must verify integrity by recomputing hashes on ingest and on verification requests.
Package identity must be deterministic and derived from content so two builds of identical content have the same identity (cross-ref PKG).
Caches (build outputs, decoded assets, precompiled code) must be keyed by content hash so cached results are safe to reuse.
Snapshots and system generations must share content-addressed objects so a new generation costs only its changed objects.
Content addressing must support reproducibility checks: a rebuilt package must be verifiable as bit-identical by hash (cross-ref BLD reproducible builds).
Packages must be stored as content-addressed objects.
Binaries must be stored as content-addressed objects.
Assets bundled with applications must be stored as content-addressed objects.
Dependencies must be stored as content-addressed objects.
System generations must be represented as content-addressed trees.
Cached build outputs from native development environments must be stored as content-addressed objects (cross-ref ENV).
Define garbage collection for the content-addressed store: root set (live generations, installed packages, pinned objects), collection policy, and user control.
Decide how the content-addressed store maps onto the chosen filesystem (hardlinked object directory, reflinked files, filesystem-native dedup) to avoid double storage.
Applications must be distributed and installed as immutable packages; installed package contents can never be mutated in place.
Define the Package manifest schema (identity, version, components, interfaces, requested capabilities, dependencies, resources).
A Package must declare its Components (entry points, code objects, per-component capability requirements).
A Package must bundle Resources (assets, localisation data) accessible via PackageData.
A Package must declare the typed Interfaces it exposes so other applications and automation can discover them (cross-ref SEM).
A Package must declare RequestedCapabilities, which drive the permissions model and install-time review (cross-ref SEC permissions UI).
A Package must declare Dependencies as content-addressed references to other immutable packages.
Implement the install operation as 'make package available': fetch objects into the content store, register the package in the current or next generation, and expose its launcher entry.
Installation must never copy shared libraries or DLL-equivalents into shared locations.
Installation must never write registry-style global configuration.
Installation must never install a background daemon implicitly; persistent services require an explicit capability grant (cross-ref §21).
Installation must never modify system configuration files.
Installation must never drop files across shared directories.
Decide the on-disk and on-wire package format (content-addressed tree with manifest vs single signed archive) and its relationship to the content store.
Packages must be signed and signatures verified before a package becomes available (cross-ref REL signing).

Define how Linux and Windows compatibility applications are packaged as immutable packages (OCI images, Flatpak-like bundles, Wine prefixes) while still satisfying the no-mutation rule (cross-ref LNX, WIN).
Implement uninstall as removing the package from the next generation without deleting content that other generations or packages still reference.
Provide package build tooling in the SDK that produces a manifest and content-addressed package from a native project.
Dependencies must be immutable objects referenced by content identity, never by mutable global name lookup.
Multiple versions of the same library must coexist (App A → Library 1.4, App B → Library 2.1) with each application bound to its own version.
There must be no global dependency conflict state; installing any package must never break another installed package.
Identical dependency objects across packages must be deduplicated automatically by the content store.
Write a verification test installing two applications with conflicting library versions and confirming both run and share no mutable state.
Decide dependency resolution semantics: exact content-hash pins in the manifest versus version ranges resolved at install time, and where lockfiles live.
Define how security fixes reach a library pinned by many packages (rebuild and republish dependents, grafting/substitution rules, or runtime relinking) without global mutation.
Decide the native linking model (static linking, dynamic linking against content-addressed shared objects, or both) and its effect on startup sharing (cross-ref §34).
Define how the native dependency model interoperates with Linux personality shared libraries (glibc, distribution libraries) that expect a global /usr/lib namespace (cross-ref LNX).
The operating system must be immutable and versioned; the running system image must not be mutated in place.
Define SystemGeneration as a kernel-visible or platform object that names one complete bootable system configuration.
A SystemGeneration must pin the kernel image and modules.
A SystemGeneration must pin the desktop shell.
A SystemGeneration must pin the compositor.
A SystemGeneration must pin all system services.
A SystemGeneration must pin the set of installed packages.
An update must create a new SystemGeneration (N+1) and leave generation N intact and bootable.
The bootloader must present and allow selection of previous generations at boot (cross-ref BOOT generation selection).
Boot failure of a new generation must be detected automatically (boot counter, health check) and the previous generation booted without user intervention.
Rollback must be a first-class operation exposed through CLI (os restore) and the settings UI, not emergency tooling.
Decide how a generation is materialised: Nix-style symlink/profile tree over the content store, filesystem snapshot per generation, or a verified image per generation.
Define what is excluded from a generation (user data, ApplicationData, logs, caches) and how mutable state is separated from the immutable image.
Implement generation garbage collection with a user-controlled retention policy for old generations.
Define atomicity of kernel plus driver plus firmware updates within a generation, including firmware that cannot be rolled back (cross-ref BOOT, HW).
Demonstrate simple system generations (create, switch, boot previous) in V0.5 per §60.
Generation images must be integrity-verified at boot against their content hashes (cross-ref BOOT measured boot, §26 integrity verification).
Measure generation creation time and disk overhead per generation and track them as standing benchmarks.
All system state changes must be recorded as explicit, typed history events in a durable log.
Implement the system history (os history) command listing events with timestamp and human-readable description.
History must record application installation events (e.g. 'Installed Blender').
History must record application update events (e.g. 'Updated IDE').
History must record development environment changes (e.g. 'Changed project environment') (cross-ref ENV).
History must record OS update events.
History must record driver update events.
Implement system restore <point> (os restore) that returns the system to the state recorded at a chosen history event.
Restore must be able to revert the OS version (generation).
Restore must be able to revert the set of installed applications.
Restore must be able to revert package versions.
Restore must be able to revert system and application configuration.
Restore must be able to revert user data via storage snapshots (cross-ref §26).
Restore must be able to revert workspaces (open projects, environments).
Restore must be able to revert application state where applications opt in to state checkpointing.
Restore must work without maintaining complete duplicate machine images; it must rely on content-addressed sharing and snapshots.
Decide which state classes (OS, apps, packages, configuration, user data, workspaces, app state) are restorable at each milestone and which are in scope for 1.0.
Define how configuration and application state are captured as versioned objects so they can participate in restore (structured settings store vs snapshotting ApplicationData).
Define selective restore (restore only apps, only OS) and how partial restore avoids inconsistent combinations.
Expose history and restore in the settings application UI (cross-ref APP, INS rollback UX).
Failure and restart semantics must be part of every typed interface design; interfaces must define client behaviour on service loss (cross-ref IPC).

Build a supervision and service-management layer (propose new workstream SVC: system services, supervision, restart policy, dependency ordering) that restarts critical user-space services and re-advertises their interfaces.

Selected GPU user-space services must be restartable where driver support permits.
Client libraries and the SDK must support detecting service disconnect on a Channel.
Client libraries must support rebinding to a restarted service instance by interface name rather than by dead endpoint.
Client libraries must support retry of idempotent Operations after rebind with defined semantics.
Client libraries must support restore-state: re-establishing session state (surfaces, streams, subscriptions) with a restarted service.
Demonstrate compositor crash → restart → surfaces rebound → applications continue rendering without restart (V0.5 service restart/rebind demo per §60).
Surface and window objects must survive compositor restart (owned by the kernel or a persistent broker) so the restarted compositor can re-attach them.
Define which compositor state (window geometry, stacking order, focus, workspace) is restored after restart and where it is checkpointed.
Where hardware or driver constraints prevent seamless recovery (e.g. GPU reset), the system must report explicit degraded recovery to the user and to clients rather than silently failing.
Build a chaos test suite that kills each restartable service under load and verifies clients rebind within a bounded time.
Decide the service naming and discovery mechanism that lets clients rebind by interface identity across restarts (kernel-held service registry vs user-space broker).
Study Erlang/BEAM supervision trees and Fuchsia component manager restart policies to design supervision strategies (one-for-one, escalation, backoff).
Measure service restart-to-rebind latency for the compositor and audio server and track as standing benchmarks.

Build a user-space driver framework providing Object<Device> capabilities, interrupt delivery as Operation completions, and DMA-capable MemoryObjects.
Evaluate and, where acceptable, implement Bluetooth host stack as a user-space driver component.
Evaluate and, where acceptable, implement selected USB device classes as user-space drivers.
Evaluate and, where acceptable, implement audio device drivers in user space with a measured latency budget (cross-ref AUD).
Evaluate and, where acceptable, implement sensor drivers as user-space components.
Implement printer drivers as user-space components.
Evaluate remaining peripheral classes (input, cameras, storage bridges) for user-space driver residency.
Run higher-level GPU services (shader compilation, allocation brokers, display management policy) in user space above the retained DRM/KMS kernel drivers (cross-ref GFX).

Document the kernel-residency decision criteria for each driver class: latency requirements, DMA safety, interrupt performance, hardware architecture constraints, and compatibility with inherited Linux drivers.
Do not pursue microkernel purity; drivers may remain in the kernel where the criteria justify it.
Decide the mechanism for user-space driver hardware access: reuse VFIO/UIO-style interfaces, or design a native Device capability with IOMMU-protected DMA via MemoryObject.
Prototype one user-space driver (e.g. a USB HID or USB audio device) and measure latency and throughput against the in-kernel Linux driver.
Define how a user-space native driver coexists with Linux personality expectations (/dev nodes, sysfs, udev events) for the same device (cross-ref LNX).

User-space drivers must require IOMMU protection for DMA so a compromised driver cannot read arbitrary physical memory.

Executables and dependencies must be memory-mapped directly from the content store at launch.

Launch metadata (component graph, capability set, relocation state) must be cached aggressively across launches.
Identical code pages across applications must be shared in memory via the content store.
Packages must support precompiled artefacts (prelinked images, precompiled shaders, AOT-compiled Wasm) stored content-addressed (cross-ref WASM).
Deduplicated dependency objects must be loaded once and shared across all applications that reference them.

Build a startup benchmark harness measuring warm and cold launch for the reference native apps (Terminal, Editor, Image Viewer) against equivalent Linux, Windows, and macOS applications (cross-ref §54).
Decide the verified-once trust mechanism for cached verification (dm-verity style block verification, signed content-store index, or per-launch hash of a small manifest).
Define the measurement boundary for 'visible UI' (first compositor presentation of a non-blank frame) so startup numbers are comparable across apps and systems.

Implement the native launch path: resolve package generation entry, create ResourceDomain, create Component, attach declared capabilities, map immutable package objects, schedule (cross-ref §53 isolation path).
Measure cold startup (content not in page cache) for simple native applications and set a target separately from the warm target.
Profile the launch path breakdown (Component creation, capability attachment, mapping, runtime init, first frame) to identify where the 20 ms budget is spent.
Implement development isolation as a native OS primitive (a DevelopmentEnvironment object composed from native primitives), not as a userspace tool layered on containers.

Do not require a Linux VM for native development environments.

Do not require Docker Desktop or any equivalent desktop VM manager for development environments.
Define and implement the environment.yaml project definition format with top-level runtime, services and resources sections.

Measure cached environment startup (os env enter on a previously built environment) and reach < 50 ms where practical.

Decide whether environment.yaml is a distinct schema or a profile of the package manifest (§28), and whether YAML or a typed manifest format is the canonical source (ADR).
Resolve how environment.yaml version specifiers (php: 8.6, postgres: 19) are locked, where the lock file lives, and how service packages are discovered in the package repository.
Resolve how the environment's NetworkNamespace exposes service endpoints (postgres, redis) to the developer's shell, IDE and browser without granting ambient network authority.
Record environment changes as system history events (§31 lists 'Changed project environment') so os history and os restore cover environments.

Development environments must be able to run Linux-personality runtimes and services (php, postgres, redis are Linux software) inside native isolation; document the dependency on LNX for environment components.

Build a reference environment.yaml demo (php + postgres + redis) that is used as the V1 acceptance test for dev environments.
OCI containers must remain supported for users.
OCI container support belongs to the Linux compatibility personality, never to the native platform.
Native software should rarely need containers; no native subsystem may depend on an OCI runtime.
Native isolation (ResourceDomain + Component + capabilities) must be measurably cheaper than OCI container isolation in creation latency and memory overhead; publish the comparison.
Integrate an OCI runtime (e.g. runc/crun via podman) inside the Linux personality using personality-provided namespaces, cgroups and overlay filesystem semantics.
Decide which container engine surface to support in the Linux personality (podman, containerd, Docker CLI/socket compatibility) (ADR).
Resolve whether Docker socket API compatibility is required for developer adoption or whether podman-compatible tooling suffices.
Prototype and measure the cost of the traditional isolation path (runtime daemon, namespace setup, overlay mount, cgroups, process startup) against the native path to validate the §53 claim.

Define the ComputeDevice native object type and its kernel ABI surface.
Expose the CPU as a ComputeDevice.

Define FPGA as a ComputeDevice class (interface definition; backend optional before 1.0).
Define a generic accelerator ComputeDevice class for vendor accelerators.

Workloads must be able to express a latency requirement/preference.
Workloads must be able to express a throughput requirement/preference.
Workloads must be able to express an energy requirement/preference.
Workloads must be able to express a precision requirement (e.g. fp32/fp16/int8).
Workloads must be able to express memory requirements.
Workloads must be able to express locality requirements relative to MemoryObjects and devices (§17).
Implement compute.dispatch(workload, preference) as an asynchronous Operation (§18, §19).
Implement a placement service that selects an appropriate ComputeDevice for a workload from its requirements and preferences.
Decide the portable workload representation for heterogeneous dispatch (SPIR-V, Wasm, native kernels per device, multiple) (ADR).
Resolve how ComputeDevice relates to Object<ComputeQueue> (§7, §39): is a queue derived from a device capability, and who owns scheduling between them.
Survey existing heterogeneous dispatch models (SYCL/oneAPI, CUDA graphs, Vulkan compute, Metal, Level Zero, ONNX Runtime EPs) before committing the ComputeDevice API.

The native ABI is the project's most permanent decision; changes to it require the highest review bar in the project.
ABI rule 1: keep the kernel ABI minimal; enumerate and bound the syscall/object-operation surface.
ABI rule 2: prefer high-level semantics in userspace services rather than in the kernel ABI.
ABI rule 3: capabilities are fundamental — every object reference crossing the ABI is a Capability<T>.
ABI rule 4: async is fundamental — no blocking syscalls in the native ABI other than explicit wait-for-completion.
ABI rule 5: ownership transfer is fundamental — the ABI carries move semantics for MemoryObjects and capabilities.
ABI rule 6: versioning is fundamental — the ABI includes version identification and feature negotiation from V0.
ABI rule 7: do not expose implementation details (task_struct, mm_struct, cgroups, namespaces, page-table layout) through the native ABI.
ABI rule 8: preserve escape hatches for future hardware (capability representation, memory model, compute devices) (cross-ref §8, §38).
ABI rule 9: avoid POSIX-shaped APIs unless independently justified; each POSIX-resembling native API requires an ADR.
ABI rule 10: design the ABI to survive decades; include a formal freeze and evolution process.
ADR: native ABI shape — syscall entry mechanism, handle table design, object-operation dispatch, error model, and ABI version negotiation.

Principle 12: semantic interfaces beat GUI automation.
